articles.title_zh: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.
Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.
A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.
The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.
Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".
It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."
Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".
It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".
Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.
He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.
Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.
More than 1,640 people have been killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Update November 15: An earlier version of this article referred to Israel carrying out 'occasional' strikes in Gaza following a ceasefire in October 2025. This word has been removed to better reflect the frequency of Israeli strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire.

articles.title_orig: Age of consent: Pat McFadden says changes to law will be 'discussed' after Brand allegations
articles.title_zh: Age of consent: Pat McFadden says changes to law will be 'discussed' after Brand allegations
articles.content_orig:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.
Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.
A woman who alleges she was raped by the jailed comedian when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16-and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.
Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."
Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds, under UK law.
Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants to see the age of consent to be staggered.
Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
She was known under the pseudonym "Alice". Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.
At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]."
"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper.
"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But… if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."
Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.
ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.
One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.
Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.
Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.
The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story.  The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".
Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pension secretary, told Kuenssberg that it was worth debating a change to age of consent laws.
Whately said she has teenage daughters and would be concerned if they brought home a man many years older than them.
"I think any parent would look twice," she said, adding: "let's have the debate".
Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC charity, said 16 and 17-year-olds can be particularly vulnerable to grooming by some adults and laws have been changed in recent years to prevent more people in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with children of such an age.
She said "other laws are failing to prevent them from being sexually exploited", adding: "Even though they are over the age of consent, young people are still entitled to be protected from harm."

articles.title_orig: PS Plus Subscriptions on Sale from Tomorrow, But There's a Big Catch
articles.title_zh: PS Plus Subscriptions on Sale from Tomorrow, But There's a Big Catch
articles.content_orig:
Sony has revealed its PS Plus membership at all three tiers will be going on sale from tomorrow, 16th November, for two weeks.
However, if you've been paying attention to how Sony handles this promotion in the last few years, then you will already know what's coming: the discounted prices only apply to new sign-ups; current members won't have access to them.
"Players in participating countries who join PlayStation Plus during PlayStation’s Black Friday promotion can save big on select memberships," Sony clarifies in an updated PlayStation Blog post . As it states, you have to "join" PS Plus during the Black Friday offer period to qualify, which lasts from 16th November to 30th November.
The only promotion open to current PS Plus members is a subscription upgrade to PS Plus Premium . Anyone at the PS Plus Essential or PS Plus Extra tiers can upgrade to PS Plus Premium at a discounted rate.
If you already are a PS Plus Premium subscriber, there quite literally isn't a single offer open to you. "Current PlayStation Plus members can also enjoy an upgrade offer on PlayStation Plus Premium/Deluxe," it says.
This is a tactic Sony has utilised for years now — it has not let you extend a PS Plus membership at the same tier for a very long time. Instead, the promotion once again only applies to PS5, PS4 owners joining PS Plus.

articles.title_orig: Beijing faces Russia bind amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
articles.title_zh: Beijing faces Russia bind amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
articles.content_orig:
An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China , Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week.
China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.
The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping .

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.
At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.
In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.
A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies , most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump . The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.
For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.
As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues , Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability .
The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.
She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.
For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival,  and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.
"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.
Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.
The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.
At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.
Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.
While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome .
"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.
"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.
In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.
However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.
Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is  concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea , which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.
But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.
MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."
"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.
Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
articles.title_zh: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: As US credit card debt hits $1.29T, bank algorithms are rejecting debt-free, six-figure earners
articles.title_zh: As US credit card debt hits $1.29T, bank algorithms are rejecting debt-free, six-figure earners
articles.content_orig:
‘The Ramsey Show’ co-host Jade Warshaw and credit repair analyst Micah Smith speak to Fox News Digital about how high-earning, low-debt consumers may face credit card and loan penalization.
Across the country, Americans earning six-figure salaries, carrying no debt and sitting on healthy savings accounts are increasingly hitting an unexpected wall when applying for everyday credit cards or loans: instant denial from automated bank algorithms.
The rejections highlight a growing rift between kitchen-table financial discipline and corporate underwriting models. While nationwide credit card balances have climbed to a record $1.29 trillion — a 67% surge since early 2021, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — data from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) shows an estimated 25 million adults have credit files "too thin" or stale to generate a standard score.
Rather than rewarding households that avoid borrowing, modern underwriting algorithms can interpret limited recent credit activity as a sign of uncertain lending risk, potentially making it harder for some debt-free consumers to qualify for credit.
"Is corporate America penalizing people who live debt-free? I would say they're not penalizing them, but they are not prioritizing them because we're not the ones making them money," Jade Warshaw, co-host of "The Ramsey Show" — who paid off $460,000 in debt alongside her husband — told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the credit score in general, the whole purpose, it's a product, and so it's out there for banks to make money. And if we're not going to be their customer, then yes, they're not going to prioritize us."
IRS ANNOUNCES 2027 TAX CHANGES: WHAT TAXPAYERS NEED TO KNOW
"Responsible, debt-free living, while it is something that we as consumers should absolutely strive for, the interesting thing about how credit works is it's very counterintuitive," credit repair specialist and Micah Abigail LLC founder Micah Smith also told Fox News Digital.
While U.S. credit card balances hit a new high, an estimated 25 million Americans have credit files considered "too thin." (Getty Images)
Smith recalled walking into a dealership as a young, debt-free adult to buy her first car, only to be told she was denied financing and needed a co-signer because lenders "couldn't see who she was on paper."
"The algorithms are looking for movement," Smith explained. "They want to see what you've actually been doing. So the interesting thing about credit is that income is never a factor into the score itself. And so you might have this incredible income, but you might not have a credit score that supports exactly who you are as a person."
A 2025 consumer study by PYMNTS Intelligence and the Federal Reserve found that credit anxiety and unexpected loan denials are no longer just low-income struggles, but they increasingly strike households earning over $100,000 due to a lack of borrowing diversity and thin credit files.
Such credit challenges can complicate applications for entry-level credit cards with major providers like Chase or Capital One, as well as financing for cars and mortgages.
Credit card debt hits a record $1.29 trillion as President Donald Trump pushes for a 10% interest rate cap, sparking rare agreement between the left and right.
Warshaw noted that Fair, Isaac and Company, the predecessor of FICO, was founded in 1956 by Bill Fair and Earl Isaac to develop credit risk analytics, not to measure personal wealth, and argued that decades of financial marketing have conditioned Americans to confuse the two.
"As American consumers, we've allowed the credit score to confuse being profitable for banks with us being actually financially good with money, and it's not the same thing," Warshaw said. "Being profitable with banks by having a good credit score does not equal being a financially responsible adult and actually having wealth and being good with money."
Smith also cautioned against "buy now, pay later" platforms as some of them have started reporting to credit bureaus. So, instead of helping with retail purchases, she warns, opening multiple short-term installment loans creates a flurry of new accounts that continuously drags down the "average age of credit" and makes a file look erratic.
"… if you owe money to anyone for any reason, that person has power over you."
"Every time you open something, it’s going to take your overall length of history backwards," Smith said. "It’s opened up as an installment loan — you open it, pay it off and it closes. So having those opened up often could suppress your scores pretty substantially."
The philosophy popularized by Dave Ramsey is that the credit score is simply an "I love debt" score that measures your relationship with lenders as opposed to true financial success. Warshaw advises consumers to cut up their cards and practice total abstinence, warning that credit cards can act as a "gateway drug" that leaves families vulnerable to financial disaster.
"If you look at all the research and data out there, you will find the research that says if you hold credit cards, you are also more likely to hold other forms of consumer debt —  so personal loans, car loans, mortgage debt, all of those things. So credit cards, in that way, it kind of is a gateway drug into the other forms of debt," Warshaw said.
Credit repair influencer and Micah Abigail LLC founder Micah Smith speaks to Fox News Digital about how to make improvements to credit scores in just 30 days, while cautioning against credit misconceptions.
"It's so easy to get behind," she continued. "And I remind people all the time, I say, 'I get it.’ Most people out there who talk to me about credit cards, they say, 'Jade, don't worry, I pay it off every single month.' And I say, 'Really, you pay it off every single month? America has $1.3 trillion in debt. That means someone's lying.'"
Smith agreed that living debt-free is an admirable goal, but argued that voluntarily becoming "invisible" in a digital economy creates expensive, everyday roadblocks when dealing with landlords and co-ops, or operating a small business. She argued, "You will not be able to run a business on cash alone. It doesn't exist."
The credit repair expert recounted a recent trip to Las Vegas where more than $9,000 in travel expenses were funded entirely through accumulated credit card points and cash back rewards.
"I think the Ramsey solution is great for people who don't have the ability to say ‘no.’ If you live responsibly, you need to have credit," Smith said. "You need to have it established because it's going to open doors that cash just won't, and that's just a fact."
The experts offer differing advice for fiscally responsible consumers: keep revolving cards open with low balances to pay off every month, or treat debt as surrendering control and build a 3-to-6-month cash emergency fund.

"The biggest thing that people don't realize is that [with] credit cards, you can have an 800 credit score with just having credit cards, and you want to maintain them. And so open them, use a small amount, pay them off," Smith said. "In the world of FICO, they actually reward tiny little balances, so leave a balance of $1 to $5. That's all you need to ensure it calculates into the credit score."
"Around here, we believe that the borrower is slave to the lender — meaning if you owe money to anyone for any reason, that person has power over you," Warshaw argued. "Credit cards aren't there to build wealth. Credit cards are there as a product to help you overspend and make banks money. But if you really want to be wealthy, son or daughter, what you're going to do is you're going to avoid debt. You're going to take your margin, and you're going to invest it for the future."

articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: BlackBerry boss on the company's evolution from smartphone giant to software powerhouse
articles.content_orig:
BlackBerry CEO John Giamatteo discusses the company’s evolution beyond smartphones and its growing focus on automotive software and secure communications.
For many people, BlackBerry still brings to mind the signature smartphone that was once a staple of corporate America.
But the BlackBerry that CEO John Giamatteo leads today looks very different.
The devices that made the brand a household name are gone. In their place is a software business whose technology largely operates behind the scenes, powering systems in cars, government communications, robotics and medical equipment while securing communications for governments and other critical organizations.
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A METEOROLOGIST BUILT A BETTER UMBRELLA
"We're a different company than we were from the device days, but we are powering with our software and services the world around us in a lot of different ways," Giamatteo told FOX Business.
For Giamatteo, continuing the reinvention of the brand has meant following a simple playbook of doing fewer things and doing them well.
"Simplify what you're doing," Giamatteo said.

articles.title_orig: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
articles.title_zh: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
articles.content_orig:
In a new report, “ Space-Based Data Centers Roadmap: The Case for Caution ,” the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum warns that space-based data centers are likely to become a reality within the next few years—well before the risks of large-scale deployment can be fully understood or governed.
Led by David Sandalow , inaugural fellow at Columbia’s Center on Global Energy Policy, the report urges companies and policymakers to proceed with great caution.
Some space-based data centers are already operating today, with proposals to launch more than 1 million data centers into orbit. According to the roadmap, neither technical challenges nor high costs are likely to stop initial deployment, since leading companies will be willing to absorb high costs for years to gain technical expertise and secure their market position.
One central concern is the scale of rocket launches required to meet the projected global demand for these centers. To put even 10% of the artificial intelligence data centers anticipated by 2030 into orbit would require more than 700 launches of large rockets every year, about two per day, in perpetuity.
The report also emphasizes the need to heed the lessons of accidents such as Deepwater Horizon and Fukushima . Policymakers should not allow the deployment of large constellations of space-based data centers until there is more operational experience and the risks and impacts are better understood and well managed, the authors warn.
Alexis Abramson , dean of the Columbia Climate School and a principal co-author, also contributed two chapters to the roadmap: “Cooling” and “Night Sky and Astronomy,” which she wrote with Sandalow.
In “Cooling,” Abramson notes that thermal management is a key issue with space-based data centers, which can shed their waste heat only by radiating it into space. The best system design, while seemingly counterintuitive, would be to run the AI-grade chips as hot as they can safely tolerate, since a hotter radiator sheds far more heat and keeps panels small and launch mass low, she writes.
However, the degradation of radiator coatings and the satellite’s debris-avoidance maneuvers could undermine thermal performance over a satellite’s lifetime—factors that might be not captured in initial analyses, Abramson points out.
The report urges developers to treat cooling as a critical design constraint and calls for standard thermal performance metrics and disclosures so that claims can be independently verified.
In “Night Sky and Astronomy,” Abramson and Sandalow warn that these large constellations of space-based data centers could cause a dramatic transformation of night skies around the world. For example, satellites could outnumber visible stars in many places. Observational astronomy and related research would be especially affected, they write. While technical measures could reduce these effects, there would be operational trade-offs and the need to radiate waste heat would persist. The report outlines a range of policy responses, including brightness limits, pre-launch impact assessments, required mitigation measures, caps on satellite numbers and international standards, that could help mitigate some of these effects.
According to the paper, there are other significant risks and impacts from space-based data centers, including large debris fields in low Earth orbit, loss of life and property damage from de-orbiting satellites, depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer and increased global warming. The current governance regimes will not be sufficient to manage these risks, especially as addressing many of the challenges will need to be coordinated on a global scale.
Other principal co-authors include Colin McCormick, chief innovation officer of Relae; Roger Aines, former energy program chief scientist and distinguished member of the technical staff at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory; Kathleen Curlee, senior research analyst at the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University; Julio Friedmann, chief scientist at Relae; and Hari Osofsky, Myra and James Bradwell professor and former dean of the Northwestern Pritzker School of Law. Contributing co-authors: Theiija Bala, J.D. candidate at Columbia Law School; Anne-Amélie Campant, Schwarzman scholar at Tsinghua University; and Alp Kucukelbir, director of artificial intelligence and supply chain optimization at Amazon.

articles.title_orig: Congress moves to pass tighter AI chip export rules following Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Congress moves to pass tighter AI chip export rules following Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The resignation of Jensen Huang , together with the results of the recent congressional election , could make this a watershed moment in the relationship of American business to government, one that sees the pendulum swing back toward greater regulation and greater separation of finance from politics.
Corruption topped the list among issues that motivated voters in the overwhelming and nationwide midterm election victory for Democrats, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. It showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision, a percentage point higher than the cost of living.
When voters were asked which party was best able to deal with the corruption issue, Democrats led Republicans 37% to 30% — though, significantly, 32% said neither party.
It's impossible to know exactly what voters mean when they say corruption, but there are hints it involves the relationship of business to government. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey, taken two weeks before the election, asked respondents if elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should personally own or trade stocks in companies that have contracts with the federal government. An overwhelming 93% said it should not be allowed . A similarly bipartisan 89% objected to the president's family members receiving government contracts.
The upshot: The very close relationship between business and the government, which has existed under both political parties but has come plainly and brazenly to the fore in President Trump's second administration, is now a major issue for voters.
The Huang affair encompasses all of that. Nvidia, along with several other large corporations, made large donations to the president's ballroom . Meanwhile, there are allegations that the administration did not act when informed of potentially illegal sales of Nvidia chips to China. It may be that the president ignored warnings from inside his own administration that Huang was involved with a woman who was reportedly a potential Chinese spy , instead bringing Huang on a state visit to China and giving him say in U.S. export policies for chips.
The Trump era has seen the virtual creation of the CEO Statesman: Huang and other tech execs draped around the president during foreign trips, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiating with Russia , Elon Musk deciding who the federal government fires.
Could the Huang affair be the end of that phenomenon?
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., wasted no time in signaling the new Congress was ready to get tough on tech execs.
"It's clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China's hands."
The enormity of Huang's fall cannot be overstated. Imagine J.P. Morgan resigning — or Jack Welch or Steve Jobs or Tim Cook. Few have stood astride the pinnacle of political and corporate power during their era like Huang during the AI boom.
This comes at a time of massive wealth increases for the elite that have helped undermine faith in capitalism. The CNBC Voter Poll showed 56% with a strong or somewhat favorable opinion of capitalism, with 32% reporting an unfavorable opinion and 12% saying they don't know.
But those numbers are overwhelmingly driven by older Americans. Younger Americans, ages 18 to 34, have a deeply negative opinion. Those aged 35 to 49 are favorable toward capitalism by only a 46%-41% margin.
What could this mean for business?
For starters, it could result in a return to more traditional separation of business and politics, where business has less of a direct say in policy. But this could be the start of a more significant change.
In the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the banking system was put under such strict regulations, many of which exist to this day, that one commentator remarked it was "in receivership in everything but name only." One can go back even further to more extreme measures taken when the public was deeply dissatisfied with business — to the fallout from the robber baron era when the trusts were busted up, or the wake of the Great Depression when the government put stricter regulations on banks and Wall Street and gave unions more power.
Democrats will be limited, even with large gains in both houses, in their ability to overturn presidential decisions with veto-proof majorities. But executives themselves may decide that it's not a good look any longer to be seen being too cozy with the White House. And some Republicans, especially those from swing states, may read the change in the electoral winds and side with Democrats on some of the most populist issues, like the data centers, the environment and even regulation.
The irony is that Trump ran, among other things, on a strong deregulatory agenda, one that business welcomed as unshackling overregulation during the Biden administration. With potential support from the public, and an overwhelmingly Democratic Congress, the pendulum may be about to swing the other way.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia's first post-Jensen earnings and Anthropic's IPO: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
As if last week couldn't have gotten any busier, the biggest business story of the year rocked investors as scandal embroiled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and forced the "godfather of AI" to step aside, a proposition that looked unthinkable only days earlier.
But lest we forget, the news cycle goes on, and this week brings its own major headline: Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO, expected to price on Wednesday and trade on Thursday.
As the first pure-play generative AI company to come to market, investors will be paying close attention to every angle.
Markets will go into a fresh week continuing the feeling of post-election whiplash, though perhaps for different AI-based reasons. But incredibly, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is almost exactly where it was before the election results as, once again, major headlines and crosscurrents have more or less canceled each other out.
Lots of action, little motion, broadly speaking.
Anthropic will dominate headlines this week, but that doesn't mean we've got an empty calendar of other news happening. On the earnings front, Nvidia ( NVDA ) (of all companies, what timing!) will report its quarterly results on Tuesday, with interim CEO Colette Kress set to helm the management call after the sudden call-up.
It's also a huge week for retail. We've got big box stores Target ( TGT ) on Wednesday, and Walmart ( WMT ) and Ross Stores ( ROST ) on Thursday, with BJ's Wholesale Club ( BJ ) rounding out the group on Friday for a check on consumer spending and outlook.
In the tech space, Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) and Bending Spoons ( BSP ) will report on Wednesday and Friday, respectively. Two of China's largest companies, Baidu ( BIDU ) and Alibaba ( BABA ), will give their own results on Monday and Thursday, respectively.
On the economic data calendar, the key readouts will be retail sales data on Tuesday and the University of Michigan's twice-monthly readout on consumer sentiment on Friday.
In a move practically unthinkable only a week ago, Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as CEO of Nvidia, the world's leading chipmaker and, up until recently, the market's most valuable company.
The headlines trickled in slowly at first before a deluge of reports revealed affairs first with a Chinese national suspected by US intelligence to be a spy for Beijing — and then with two Nvidia employees.
Here's a big rundown of all the news.
While the board looks for a permanent replacement, CFO Colette Kress has taken up the mantle as interim CEO, with tons of open questions facing the company Huang founded more than 30 years ago.
Perhaps chief among those is who can replace the man who has more or less single-handedly driven Nvidia forward since its inception and become the face of the AI trade —and bull market.
The news of Huang's entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy — which comes after years of forceful comments from the disgraced CEO that Nvidia should be able to sell its best chips into China — has also led members of Congress to call a series of hearings.
Over the next month, Huang, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter, and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick are all expected to testify and answer questions from both chambers of Congress about not only Huang's conduct, but potential violations of US export policy.
It's safe to say that there's a lot of confusion swirling around a company that reports earnings this week. As our tech editor Daniel Howley writes, this past week's upheaval won't impact earnings this quarter or next . Nvidia has sales locked in well in advance, meaning its bottom line won't take a hit for some time, if at all.
That said, Kress will have to acknowledge Huang's departure and the company's plans moving forward during the call. And analysts will have plenty of questions, as a number of analysts have already either downgraded or cut their price targets on Nvidia stock.
Baird Equity Research analyst Tristan Gerra said Huang's resignation turns a page for Nvidia but that the episode hasn't hit its bottom yet.
"Headwinds include potential incremental senior management departures, H200 write-down charges, potential risk channel revenue adjustments, potential litigation [and] fines, uncertainties until [a] new CEO is announced along with the risk of some market share loss in 2029 as customers make contingency plans on a major top management transition and looking beyond the current product roadmap, along with more clarity on the next CEO's views regarding customer financings," Gerra wrote in an investor note Thursday.
Ladies and gentlemen, start your engines. It's time for one of the most anticipated IPOs of the year.
Anthropic will price its initial public offering (IPO) on Wednesday, Nov. 18, the company announced Thursday . It will begin trading under the Nasdaq ticker symbol "ANT" on Thursday, Nov. 19, providing the next major test for the AI trade and could set the standard for rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) own public markets debut, which is anticipated for early next year.
In an amended S-1 filing released Tuesday , Anthropic said it expects to sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78. That would give the company a market valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Anthropic was initially projected to hit the market with a valuation as high as $2 trillion, but recent market turmoil in the AI sector has knocked that down significantly.
For the first nine months of the year ending Sept. 30, Anthropic said revenue grew $1,206% to $33.2 billion. But the AI giant also revealed a staggering aggregate committed spend of $895.4 billion , which it says is primarily related to compute and infrastructure.
Also of note: Jensen Huang's former company is tied to the IPO. Nvidia ( NVDA ) is set to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic through a private placement ahead of the IPO, per Anthropic's prospectus . That investment is set to be matched only by that of Alphabet ( GOOG ), which is also pegged to invest $10 billion in what is expected to be a $26 billion private placement, with the remaining $6 billion coming from a group of other Big Tech firms, including Broadcom ( AVGO ), Micron ( MU ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
Having a major anchor such as Nvidia on board for the IPO would usually give investors confidence in the strength of the offering. The recent scandal surrounding Jensen Huang could rattle that sense of security.
Last week's inflation readings showed both consumer and wholesale prices heat up, worrying signs for the inflation fight. But read another way, they're also potential signs that, once again, the US consumer is proving indefatigable.
The 6.5% year-over-year increase in prices producers are paying — factories, farmers, and pre-consumers in the supply chain — is another data point showing elevated pricing pressure as oil costs trickle through the economy.
The initial read on all this: December's Fed hike looks even more likely, and next year may see even more action from the Fed.
With Walmart, Target, and other big retailers reporting this week, as well as another check on consumer sentiment and government retail sales data, we'll finish the week with a much better picture of the demand side of the consumer and retail stories.
Is the economy still K-shaped? Are consumers trading down more, turning to cheaper brands?
This is especially critical given how a strong consumer has been a positive buffer and counterweight to other negative market forces over the past few years.

articles.title_orig: Empty nesters moved out of their Florida home to travel in an RV full time. They're in year five and loving it.
articles.title_zh: Empty nesters moved out of their Florida home to travel in an RV full time. They're in year five and loving it.
articles.content_orig:
Barry and Darlene Nicholson, who met as teenagers in Indiana, spent most of their lives raising their two kids in Florida, not traveling much out of state.
Since downsizing from their Florida house to become full-time RVers in 2022, they've been to around 30 states. They'd been to places they never considered visiting before, which turned out to be some of their favorites.
With their daughter soon starting college, they realized they wouldn't need their large Florida home anymore. Since home prices were rising during the pandemic, they decided it was time to start a life on the road.
The couple, who are in their 50s, wanted to experience RV life while they were still young and physically able. "My inspiration for doing it early and making it work is that you're not guaranteed tomorrow," Darlene said. "You're not guaranteed a retirement."
Their first year involved learning to drive an RV and getting used to living in a smaller space as a couple.
Even though they've been married for decades, Barry said the switch can be "a shock to both of your systems" because everyone has a routine they've been used to. Barry used to play in a band, but that stopped when they hit the road. They also learned while going through the Smoky Mountains that Darlene has travel anxiety.
They said if you're doing this lifestyle with someone else, you both have to be all in or it won't work out.
"We told people, if you can survive the first six months, you'll be fine," Darlene said.
They didn't sell their home right away; they wanted to use it as a backup plan if they ended up hating this pivot. They rented it out their first year, but after the tenants left, it was hard to find someone to rent for the same amount. They sold it in 2023.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
While they didn't sell their home before traveling, they did sell and give away a lot of their belongings. They recommend starting to downsize two years early if you can, because for them it came down to the last few days.
"It really forces you to become a minimalist," Barry said.
While they said RV life isn't as expensive as owning a home , they still spent a lot of money on experiences in the places they visit.
"We didn't want to change our lifestyle," Darlene said. "We still wanted to go out to eat. We wanted to experience things. We wanted to take tours. We wanted to do all this stuff. So we kind of just subbed one thing for the other."
Darlene planned out the entire first year in advance, booking RV park stays. They ended up, Barry said, staying in a lot of high-end RV resorts and campgrounds, spending at least $1,000 a month. But since then, they have lowered their costs as they pivoted more to boondocking, or being off-grid and providing your own electricity and water.
They installed solar panels on the RV in 2023, which helped them cut costs and live more off-grid after Darlene was let go from her job the following year. Barry said it's hard to justify the cost of a solar panel setup if you're not going to do RV life full time or do boondocking.
They don't have a washer and dryer by choice, and they pay for a service to still get mail.
While boondocking came out of necessity, Darlene said going off-grid camping has been better for them anyway, and it's helping them cut down on costs.
"We just love the peace and quiet," Barry said. "We've stayed in some places where we're surrounded by this beauty, and there's no sound other than the wind and the trees."
They're on their second RV, a 40-foot fifth wheel. October was the most they've spent on diesel; they estimate they spent more than $1,000 last month, and less than $400 a month in early 2026.
Darlene said people should have a few thousand dollars on hand in case of "what if" situations, such as needing to replace tires or needing more money for diesel.
"You got to have that backup flexibility for when these weird things happen, and you can be ready for it, and it doesn't wreck your whole plan, but that's part of this lifestyle," Darlene said. "You have to know that it's going to have all those fluctuations."
They still stay at campgrounds and RV parks from time to time. Campground costs can vary depending on where you stay and how many nights you stay. For instance, their 40-night stay at one campground cost over $2,000. Meanwhile, seven nights at an RV park elsewhere cost $288; they were off-grid the rest of that month.
Darlene searched for a new job but decided to stop given the tough job market.
"It was just trying to find a job in my 50s competing against people in their 20s and 30s who are hungry and young, and I just was really hitting my head against the wall," she said.
They have a YouTube channel they started in December 2023 called "Like There's No Tomorrow," where they talk about RV life and what they've learned as a couple who have never done this lifestyle before. The channel became monetized slightly before Darlene's job cut. Darlene said she would give the channel three months to see if they could bring in enough money to replace at least half of her income, and if not, she would go back to work. Barry left his job in 2025 and does YouTube and other content creation full time with Darlene.
When they sold their house in 2023, they invested the proceeds and don't touch it.
"I always tell people, you got to have an exit plan if you're going to do something like this because you never know what can happen," Darlene said.
That could include unexpected repairs or unexpected health problems.
When they were parked on a hillside, Darlene was dumping water in the dark one night, caught her toe on something, fell forward to push open the side patio gates, and hit her head on the ground 10 feet below. She lost feeling in her hands for about a month, had a concussion, whiplash, and fractured her skull. Another time, their dog Hugo ate something he shouldn't have and got really sick.
"Not only do you have to think about you're also not close to your local doctor, you're not close to your local vet either," Barry said.
They also want to be prepared for when their full-time RV journey ends.
"We have money put away for when we decide we are going to leave the road, and we meet with our financial planner a lot to try to make sure we're continuing to put back enough money," Darlene said. "We have goals someday of coming off the road or being a part-time traveler and not a full-time traveler with some sort of home base eventually, but it's not right now."

articles.title_orig: Ground Stop Ripples Into Third Day of Scrapped Flights
articles.title_zh: Ground Stop Ripples Into Third Day of Scrapped Flights
articles.content_orig:
In some ways, America’s air traffic control system performs far better than one might think — even if it would be tough to convince the more than one million passengers who had their travel plans upended in recent days.
It handles a huge airspace and more than 45,000 flights a day. Yet, failures are exceedingly rare, even when its antiquated equipment breaks down.
The current system uses strips of paper with the names of flights on them to be handed off from one controller to another, floppy computer discs and copper wire to handle communications for nearly a third of the system.
Experts say that fixing a system this large is a tall order, partly because the current system is so old.
“If you own a car for 30 years, it’s going to be increasingly difficult as the car gets older to find the replacement parts you need to keep it in operating condition. The same is true of any kind of technology serving any kind of industry,” said Henry Harteveldt, president of Atmosphere Research Group and a travel industry analyst. “There are many parts of airline and aviation technology that are no longer fit due to their age.”
And Friday afternoon, the painstaking efforts to keep that antiquated air traffic control system functioning caught up with the Federal Aviation Administration and the more than one million on-board and would-be passengers.
The problems arose when a contractor was working to replace some of the copper wire with fiber optics.
“That new equipment, new technology just was overwhelming the older system,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “The patchwork doesn’t work.”
The part of the air traffic control system that monitors and communicates with planes at their cruising altitude was no longer reliable enough to keep those planes in the air or allow new planes to take off. So, the FAA ordered a rare systemwide “ground stop,” leading to 9,200 canceled flights, according to tracking service FlightAware.
And even though the ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, many flights could not be started at that point due to staffing issues or the lack of planes being in the right city. So another 6,200 were canceled on Saturday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem is coming up with a modern system while keeping the current antiquated system up and running.
“I don’t want to lie to anybody,” he said Friday night at the same press conference. “What we’re doing is hard, and it hasn’t happened in the past because it is hard. But I’ll tell you, by doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system.
“We use 1980s technology, 1990s software, to use 1970s radar that we don’t make parts for anymore,” he said.
Friday’s ground stop wasn’t the first time the aging infrastructure has disrupted travel.
Communication issues with the air traffic control systems directing flights around heavily trafficked Newark Liberty Airport in May 2025 caused the FAA to limit the number of flights and resulted in air traffic controllers becoming so stressed from not being able to communicate with planes that some workers took trauma leave, causing a staffing shortage to worsen.
In a similar situation to Friday’s grounding of flights, in January 2023, the system used to notify pilots of their route’s conditions went down, grounding all flights.
It’s not just the FAA that copes with older technology. Even the actual airlines use outdated tools.
In July 2024, an automatic update from cybersecurity software provider CrowdStrike caused massive problems on Windows computers, which impacted companies all around the world and required a restart of computers. But no company had a harder time restarting normal operations than Delta Air Lines, which had greater problems bringing its crew-tracking software back online, leaving it unable to staff airplanes.
A massive problem at Southwest Airlines during the 2022 year-end holidays resulted in 16,700 canceled flights, millions of passengers scrambling to complete their holiday travel and costing the airline at least $1 billion. Much of it was due to problems with its own antiquated crew scheduling system, which required phone calls between the airline and crew members rather than online check-ins — a system that would make it impossible for the airline to find the crews it needed to staff flights.
Harteveldt, the travel analyst, said Southwest has spent at least $1.3 billion  since then upgrading its technology, hardware, software and communications networks.
“We have a much better understanding of our crew network and are able to work in real time to adjust to unexpected circumstances,” Southwest said Saturday in response to a question about its upgrades.
Airlines can be reluctant to fund back-office technology upgrades when they can instead spend on ways to attract more passengers, such as better Wi-Fi, newer planes and upgraded airport lounges, said Harteveldt.
“They are risk-averse, and so they want to be sure that whatever technology they do end up investing in is a technology that will be useful long term to the airline,” he said. “That’s another reason why airlines tend to be technology laggards. They also just don’t have the profit margins, even in the best of years, to allocate large sums to technology upgrades.”
The FAA’s problems are strictly political: it needs Congress to approve funding. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades, and before Friday, Duffy had asked for another $30 billion. On Friday night, he said the agency now needs $50 billion.
It’s possible the mess at the nation’s airports on Friday night will help win support for that greater Congressional spending. But the problems have existed for years. And even if the FAA has unlimited funds, it’s clear from the problems created by Friday’s attempted upgrade of existing systems that it won’t be repeated in the future.
“Is this exact thing going to happen again? I don’t know,” Duffy said. “I think there’s no better time than the present to actually give us the money and let us finish.”

articles.title_orig: Putin's alleged grandson avoids 'Volodymyr Zelensky' surname by taking mother's name
articles.title_zh: Putin's alleged grandson avoids 'Volodymyr Zelensky' surname by taking mother's name
articles.content_orig:
A son reportedly born to Russian President Vladimir Putin ’s daughter Katerina Tikhonova was registered under his mother’s surname rather than that of his presumed father, ballet dancer Igor Zelensky, according to Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
The dancer shares a surname with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky but is not related to him. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Agentstvo based its report on leaked civil registry records, according to Meduza, an independent Russian-language news outlet. The records indicated that Tikhonova had a son in 2025 and that his birth was registered nearly a year later. Meduza described Igor Zelensky as the presumed father.
The boy was registered with the masculine form of his mother’s surname, Tikhonov. His patronymic, a name derived from a father’s first name, was also included in the records cited by the outlets.
The Daily Mail reported that the child was given his mother’s surname to avoid the association with Ukraine’s president. The underlying reporting, however, does not establish why the name was chosen or that anyone barred the use of Zelensky. The reason for the reported delay in registration is also unknown.
Earlier reporting linked Tikhonova to the dancer. In 2022, an investigation by Russian outlet iStories and Germany ’s Der Spiegel found evidence that the two were in a long-term relationship and appeared to have a child together, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project reported.
Igor Zelensky previously led the Bavarian State Ballet in Munich. The Guardian also reported on the investigation at the time, noting that he was unrelated to the Ukrainian president.
Putin has kept details of his family largely out of public view. The latest account of the child’s birth and registration rests on the records cited by Agentstvo; the other outlets’ reports do not independently verify them.

articles.title_orig: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
articles.title_zh: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
articles.content_orig:
MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.
The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.
Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.
The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They are also expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.
The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds.
“That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay.
Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.”
But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China.
ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea.
Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials.
Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said.
He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.”
China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang's daughter was on the rise inside Nvidia. Succession may have come too soon.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's daughter was on the rise inside Nvidia. Succession may have come too soon.
articles.content_orig:
Madison Huang has emerged as an increasingly powerful figure inside Nvidia, just as the company searches for her father's successor .
Huang, daughter of former CEO Jensen Huang , has rapidly risen to the role of senior director of product marketing for physical AI and has accumulated influence far beyond her title, former employees told Business Insider. After joining the company in 2020, one said they began to see her influence expand in late 2023.
"Madison is her father's daughter — she's flinty, she's sharp, she's not a wallflower," another former employee said. "She's out there in front asking questions and changing things."
She could assume an even bigger leadership role at Nvidia in the future, two former employees said, but lacks the technical experience to replace her father now that a successor is needed. Huang's background is predominantly in business and marketing. One said they could have imagined her taking the helm in a decade, but did not have the expertise to guide Nvidia's technology strategy anytime soon.
An Nvidia colleague said Huang could strongly hold her own in technical discussions without an engineering background. They said her role is to help shape how Nvidia brings its technology to market.
The scrutiny comes as Jensen Huang exits Nvidia amid revelations of extramarital affairs and a board investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort .
In addition to choosing a new CEO, Nvidia now faces questions about how to reorganize its leadership .
"We don't know exactly how it's going to be reconfigured, but obviously things will have to change," Huang's colleague added.
Huang isn't the only family member at Nvidia. Her brother Spencer Huang works in robotics as a director of product management. Two former employees described him as having a lower profile than his sister.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
A classically trained chef, Huang has said she initially planned to study electrical engineering like her parents, but her father encouraged her to pursue something she was "really passionate about."
She attended the Culinary Institute of America, worked as a chef and sommelier, and later moved into hospitality marketing at luxury conglomerate LVMH before joining Nvidia as an MBA intern in 2020.
According to Nvidia's annual filing, she took home $1.23 million in compensation this last fiscal year. Huang's husband, Nico Caprez, also works at Nvidia as vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.
Huang has become increasingly visible outside the company. During a trip to South Korea this spring, she met with executives from tech giants such as Samsung and SK Hynix and spoke to students at Seoul National University, where she described leadership as "being in service of others."
Huang said working at Nvidia was initially "very intimidating for me because I have no technical background and I'm surrounded by the world's greatest engineers." She kept a running Google Doc of unfamiliar terms and spent hours after work researching them.
"You have to have some self-resilience and commit yourself to educating yourself on the side," she said at Seoul National University.
Her reach extends into Nvidia's startup ecosystem. Genspark cofounder Wen Sang praised her for supporting smaller AI companies and told Business Insider that she introduced his company to Nvidia's chief marketing officer for a product pitch opportunity.
She has taken on a role in major Nvidia partnerships, including collaborations with Foxconn to use AI to design and automate factories and with LG on robotics and data centers.
An Nvidia partner who works closely with Huang said she was a "driving force" in establishing a technology standards group called the Alliance for OpenUSD, and helped guide technical discussions among members.
"There is depth, there is breadth, and there is most definitely technical knowledge," they said.
Huang's colleague at Nvidia said her responsibilities have become increasingly cross-functional because of her ability to coordinate product launches across engineering, marketing, and other teams.
"She's probably, after Jensen, the hardest-working person I've ever seen in my life," they said.
Her close relationship with her father has also given her a unique edge. One former employee cited her ability to anticipate his needs while traveling with him to high-level meetings and appearances, while another said she had become a point of contact for employees seeking access to him.
"She's like a little mini Jensen, his eyes and ears inside the business," a third former employee said.
Her growing influence has changed how some teams operate, and she has also clashed with Nvidia veterans and senior executives, three former employees said.
Nvidia traditionally empowered a project's designated leader, known as the "pilot in command," to make decisions, one person said. They added that as Huang gained influence, teams sometimes put off decisions until she joined meetings, even when senior executives or subject-matter experts were present.
Huang's colleague at Nvidia said that disagreements are common and employees are encouraged to pursue "intellectual honesty."
"She's humble, she's collaborative," the Nvidia partner said, "but most definitely you know things are going to get done."

President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."
